Philemon is a Pauline associate addressed directly in Paul's epistle.
Epaphras is named by Paul as his fellow servant and fellow prisoner.
Onesiphorus is commended by Paul as a faithful supporter who sought him out in Rome.
Onesimus, converted by Paul, became his helper and is sent back as a beloved brother.
Phoebe is the deaconess and benefactor commended by Paul who carried his letter to Rome.
Junia is a kinswoman and fellow prisoner of Paul, greeted as notable among the apostles.
Ananias of Damascus baptized Saul and restored his sight, an early figure in Paul's calling.
Paul was brought up at the feet of Gamaliel, taught in the strict manner of the Law (Acts 22:3).
Cornelius's conversion as the first Gentile convert came through Peter (Acts 10).
Tabitha was raised from the dead by Peter at Joppa (Acts 9:36-42).
The Ethiopian eunuch was instructed and baptized by Philip the Evangelist (Acts 8:26-39).
Agabus is the named Christian prophet of Acts, exemplifying the gift of prophecy.
Abu Hanifa is the eponymous founder of the Hanafi school.
Malik ibn Anas is the eponymous founder of the Maliki school.
al-Shafi'i is the eponymous founder of the Shafi'i school.
Ahmad ibn Hanbal is the eponymous founder of the Hanbali school.
As founder of a school of fiqh, Abu Hanifa is an authority over Islamic legal knowledge.
As founder of a school of fiqh and compiler of the Muwatta, Malik presides over religious-legal knowledge.
al-Shafi'i systematized usul al-fiqh and presides over the science of Islamic legal knowledge.
As founder of a school of fiqh and master traditionist, Ahmad ibn Hanbal presides over hadith and legal knowledge.
